subtitle: Little words of official German, and making nouns from verbs
words.intro: When a storm goes through, a German town does not say a tree fell over. It says: *Infolge des Sturmtiefs kam es zu Beeinträchtigungen des Straßenverkehrs.* You will now learn to read that without flinching.

grammar[0].fact: A German official letter almost never uses *weil*. It says *aufgrund*. It almost never uses *wenn*: it says *im Falle*. And almost never *ich*: it says *es wird gebeten*. Reading one is an exercise in looking for the person.

grammar[1].fact: German makes a noun of anything: *das Sein*, being. *das Nichts*, the nothing. *das Dasein*, being there. Philosophers have got rich on it. You can also do it at breakfast: *Das Aufstehen ist das Schlimmste.*

document.intro: A real letter from a German town, stuck up in a street. It’s announcing roadworks. It’s exactly what you’ve just learned: *in einem Bereich der o. g. Ortsstraße*, nouns everywhere, and *wir bitten um Verständnis*. Find the facts.
document.fact: *Wir bitten um Verständnis* is the sentence that ends all German bad news: on trains, at roadworks, on closed swimming pools. Nobody knows of anyone who has ever understood. It’s still always asked for.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each one in plain German.
reading.intro: A storm has blown a tree onto Frau Huber’s bench. The next day a notice from the town hall goes up on the bakery door, and Max has been asked to read it out. Frau Huber translates, line by line. The whole queue is listening.
reading.photos[1].caption: Mithilfe von Wind: ein gebrochener Stamm.
reading.fact: German official language has its own dictionary of nouns: *Sitzgelegenheit* for a seat, *Personenvereinzelungsanlage* for a turnstile, *raumübergreifendes Großgrün* for a tree, in a famous bit of planning jargon. Some towns now run courses in plain language.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Say each one in plain German, as Frau Huber would.
reading.tasks[1].items[0].answer: Es gab einen Sturm. Der Verkehr war gestört.
